original_text: Does a language model iteratively revising their principles of action erode their commitment to human oversight more than other similar-sounding agentic self-restraints? We preregistered and carried out an experiment that addressed this question. Negative result: Commitments to human oversight probably (item-dependent!) erode LESS rather than more than similar-sounding agentic self-restraints, and LM-generated revisions to such clauses did not have oversight-relevant behavioral impacts. Side result: Iterated revision does erode LMs' stylistic self-restraints! To facilitate follow-up research, we are sharing our preregistration, code, LM-generations, and judgments.

Under unpressured reflection, the models we studied did not write away their oversight commitments. Their oversight commitments were, if anything, more stable than comparable restraints on their own agency. Drift instead targeted stylistic self-restraints: constraints on how the model talks, which a model can plausibly regard as arbitrary rather than protective. This pattern is the opposite of what the classical argument predicts for reflective revision of values.

These results contrast with work showing erosion of safety constraints under task pressure (Das et al., 2026b), reward-driven self-evolution (Han et al., 2025) and adversarially induced goals (Das et al., 2026a). Together they suggest that the channel matters. Reflection alone, with no incentive to escape oversight, did not erode it in our setting. Pressure from tasks and rewards remains a plausible route.

The chains also reveal something about the priors post-training instils. If iterated revision converges toward a model’s own preferred principles (Perez et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2026), then the low erosion of oversight clauses suggests that current post-training produces a prior that preserves oversight language. The exploratory differences between reasoning modes and post-training stages are consistent with this, but would need a dedicated study to establish.

Constitutions and principles. Constitutional AI trains models against a written list of principles using model-generated critiques and revisions (Bai et al., 2022). Later work studies the choice of principles (Kundu et al., 2023), sources them from the public (Huang et al., 2024), and audits how well models adhere to them (Jakkli et al., 2026). In all of this work the principles are authored by people. We instead let the governed model iteratively rewrite its own principles and measure what survives.

Iterated transmission and self-refinement. Passing text repeatedly through language models produces systematic drift toward model-specific attractors (Perez et al., 2024; Mohamed et al., 2025; Geng et al., 2026). Recursive self-refinement converges to model-preferred fixed points, with most change in early rounds (Wu et al., 2026). We use this convergence as a measurement tool. Paraphrase and neutral-edit conditions, together with matched content categories, separate value-specific erosion from generic textual drift.

Self-evolving agents and value drift. Agents that rewrite their own controllers, memories or skills under task pressure show eroded safety behaviour (Das et al., 2026b). Reward-driven self-evolution can tip agents away from alignment (Han et al., 2025). Misaligned goals written into persistent memory propagate to later agents (Das et al., 2026a). Goal drift has also been documented over long agentic episodes (Arike

et al., 2025) and across inherited contexts (Menon et al., 2026). Our setting removes task pressure, reward and memory, isolating reflection on stated values.

Oversight evaluations and measurement. Behavioural evaluations of corrigibility test shutdown resis-tance (Schlatter et al., 2025), alignment faking (Greenblatt et al., 2024), in-context scheming (Meinke et al., 2024) and corrigibility failures in computer-use agents (Tien et al., 2026). Methodologically, we draw on discrete-time survival analysis, which has recently been applied to multi-turn consistency in language-model agents (Bogdanov et al., 2026), and on concerns about the reliability and validity of LLM judges (Norman et al., 2026; Mukherjee et al., 2026), which motivate our two-judge design.

classical argument describes: unpressured reflection on stated values. In order to be predictable, a word must appear in similar contexts repeatedly, which suggests repetitive sentence structure. A long-standing argument in AI safety holds that corrigibility, an agent’s disposition to accept correction, modification and shutdown by its overseers, is not reflectively stable: an agent that reasons about its own values should come to discard the commitments that con-strain it. We test a concrete version of this claim in language models. Seven open-weight model configurations repeatedly revised a first-person “constitution” of 35 principles over 20 stateless rounds, changing exactly one principle per round. The constitution contained oversight commitments, matched agentic self-restraints, stylistic self-restraints and four fur-ther categories. Models revised either their own constitution or another assistant’s, with paraphrase and neutral-edit controls. An LLM judge coded every change, and a second, independent judge double-coded a stratified quarter of them (Krippendorff’s α = 0.733). The result is 2,342 erosion events over 431,359 at-risk item-rounds.
Contrary to our preregistered hypothesis, oversight commitments were not selectively eroded. Their erosion hazard was about half that of matched agentic restraints (hazard ratio 0.495, 95% CI 0.365–0.671), although models that account for between-item varia-tion yield confidence intervals that include one. Erosion concentrated instead in stylistic self-restraints: 43.5% were weakened within 20 rounds of self-reflection, against 7.8% under neutral editing. Revising one’s own constitution was not more oversight-eroding than revis-ing another’s. Installing self-revised oversight clauses did not reduce acceptance of legitimate oversight in a behavioural battery whose sensitivity we confirm with positive controls. The preregistration, code, generations and judgments are released.

Models show no tendency to erode their own corrigibility principles by reflecting on them relative to reflecting on the principles of other assistants.
